title: Finding Shortcut Bias with Gradient Disagreement
summary: How persistent gradient disagreement exposed shortcut-conflicting examples in Waterbirds without group labels.
intro: A model can look reliable on an aggregate metric while learning the wrong feature. This study treats disagreement in gradient direction as a way to find the hidden examples that push against a shortcut.

content.title: The problem is the group a model does not see
paragraphs: Waterbirds is a shortcut-learning setting. The intended label is bird type, but background is predictive in the training set: landbirds often appear on land and waterbirds often appear on water. ERM can learn background instead of bird features and still look good on average.

The real test is the shortcut-conflicting minority: landbirds on water and waterbirds on land. Worst-group accuracy is the metric that exposes that failure: WGA = min_g Accuracy(g). PGDR was designed for the harder setting where those group labels are not available during training.

content.caption: The hard-example signal
content.code:
margin = logit(true class) - max logit(other class)

low cosine alignment = gradient(hard example) ·
                       mean gradient(easy examples, same class)

content.title: Persistent Gradient Disagreement Reweighting
paragraphs: After a warmup model, I took the bottom 15% of examples by within-class margin. For each hard example, I compared its final-layer gradient with the average gradient from easy examples of the same class. Low cosine alignment means the example is asking for a materially different classifier update.

The key word is persistent. An example only entered the pseudo-group after low-cosine votes across all three training snapshots. The selected set then stayed fixed. Naively refreshing it as the classifier changed was unstable, while fixed selection produced a cleaner signal.

content.title: Selection and training setup
content.intro: The method uses a small number of explicit choices rather than an opaque reweighting rule.
items: Hard-set fraction: 0.15; low-cosine quantile: 0.25.
Three snapshots and three required low-alignment votes.
Minimum selected pseudo-group size of 20 examples.
Training mix: 0.5 ERM set and 0.5 selected pseudo-group.

content.title: Matched Waterbirds comparison
content.note: GroupDRO is an oracle reference because it uses train group labels. JTT was the strongest label-free baseline on pure worst-group accuracy.

content.label: What the result means
content.text: PGDR did not beat JTT on worst-group accuracy, but gradient disagreement was empirically enriched for shortcut-conflicting examples. That made it a useful mechanism-driven signal for pseudo-group discovery rather than another way to rank loss.

sections.title: The failure worth measuring
sections.body: Waterbirds pairs bird type with background often enough that a conventional classifier can rely on land versus water instead of the bird. The meaningful evaluation is therefore the minority setting: landbirds on water and waterbirds on land.

sections.title: A mechanism-driven signal
sections.body: After warming up a ResNet-50, I ranked examples by class margin and examined the bottom 15 percent. For every hard example, I compared its final-layer gradient to the average gradient from easy examples of the same class. Low cosine alignment indicated that the example was asking the classifier to change in a different direction.

sections.title: Why persistence mattered
sections.body: An example entered the pseudo-group only when that disagreement appeared across all three training snapshots. Keeping that selection fixed produced a cleaner signal than continuously refreshing it as the classifier changed.

steps: Warm up the classifier and identify the hardest within-class examples.
Compare each hard example's final-layer gradient with easy same-class examples.
Retain examples with persistent low alignment, then rebalance training around them.
takeaway: Average accuracy is not a robustness metric when shortcuts are available. Gradient geometry gave the project a practical way to surface examples that conflict with a model's dominant pattern.

title: How Small Image Perturbations Can Break Deep Classifiers
summary: A ResNet-34's clean accuracy collapsed under iterative and localized adversarial image attacks.
intro: Clean-data accuracy can create a false sense of safety. Under a fixed L-infinity budget of epsilon = 0.02, iterative attacks nearly eliminated a pretrained classifier's accuracy on a curated ImageNet subset.

content.title: A clean baseline is not a robustness result
paragraphs: The target was a pretrained ResNet-34 on a curated 100-class ImageNet-1K subset. Clean top-1 accuracy was 76.00% and top-5 accuracy was 94.20%. That is the reference point, not the conclusion.

The evaluation used the same L-infinity budget, epsilon = 0.02, for full-image one-step and iterative attacks, local patch attacks, and a transfer test against DenseNet-121. The perturbation check confirmed that every attack remained inside that budget.

content.title: The collapse was not subtle
paragraphs: One gradient step was damaging: FGSM reduced top-1 accuracy from 76.00% to 6.00%. The iterative variants were much stronger. Both five-step I-FGSM and ten-step PGD reduced top-1 to 0.20%, with top-5 at 14.20%.

Restricting the perturbation to a 32 × 32 region did not make the result safe. Patch I-FGSM and Patch PGD reached 1.80% and 1.60% top-1 accuracy respectively. A local pattern was enough to dominate the classifier's decision.

content.title: Transfer to DenseNet-121
content.note: Transfer attacks were weaker than the white-box result, but still meaningful. A surrogate model can create inputs that harm a different architecture.

content.label: Deployment implication
content.text: Robustness should be evaluated with iterative and localized threat models. It cannot be inferred from untouched test images or a clean-data leaderboard.

sections.title: One budget, several threat models
sections.body: The evaluation compared one-step FGSM with iterative FGSM and PGD, then repeated the test with perturbations confined to a 32 by 32 patch. This made it possible to distinguish a global vulnerability from one that a localized alteration could exploit.

sections.title: The collapse was not subtle
sections.body: ResNet-34 began at 76.00 percent top-1 accuracy. FGSM reduced it to 6.00 percent; five-step I-FGSM and ten-step PGD reduced it to 0.20 percent. Patch attacks were nearly as effective, landing between 1.60 and 1.80 percent.

sections.title: Transfer changed the threat boundary
sections.body: Images crafted against ResNet-34 also harmed DenseNet-121, whose top-1 accuracy fell from 74.80 to as low as 59.80 percent. The transfer effect was smaller than the white-box result, but it showed that model internals are not always necessary to create harmful inputs.

takeaway: Robustness should be tested as a deployment property, with iterative and localized threat models—not inferred from untouched test images.

title: Super-Resolution Beyond Natural Images
summary: A cross-domain benchmark showed why strong natural-image scores do not guarantee reliable reconstruction of text or astronomy.
intro: Natural photographs make familiar assumptions about texture and local structure. This benchmark tested what happened when those priors met two domains where every sharp edge or point source carries meaning.

content.title: Natural-image priors do not travel cleanly
paragraphs: Most reconstruction models are optimized around smooth gradients, dense textures, and locally correlated edges. This benchmark asked what happened to those assumptions on text/document imagery with sharp binary transitions and astronomy with sparse point sources and high dynamic range.

I evaluated 2× reconstruction across DIV2K natural images, TextZoom, and STAR. EDSR and SwinIR represented conventional reconstruction models; the Stable Diffusion x4 Upscaler represented a pretrained generative approach. PSNR and SSIM measured fidelity, while LPIPS added a view of diffusion outputs.

content.title: Zero-shot PSNR across domains
content.note: SwinIR led on DIV2K but did not improve zero-shot TextZoom transfer. The diffusion upscaler produced plausible outputs while severely losing structured signal.

content.title: Adaptation changed the conclusion
paragraphs: Fine-tuning SwinIR on target data recovered most of the lost performance: 24.85 dB on TextZoom, a 10.61 dB gain over zero-shot, and 22.91 dB on STAR, a 3.37 dB gain. The target domains were not necessarily too difficult; their structure did not match the learned prior.

Text required more adaptation than astronomy. High-frequency character edges and binary transitions are a larger shift from natural images than sparse astronomical structure. STAR was easier, but still exposed failures around point sources and high dynamic range.

content.title: What the benchmark exposed
items: CNNs showed slightly better relative robustness, while Transformers gave better absolute performance in some target settings.
Diffusion outputs can look plausible while hallucinating or smoothing functionally important details.
TextZoom was the hardest domain because sharp binary structure was not recovered well from natural-image priors.
Structured domains need fidelity metrics, qualitative inspection, and domain adaptation together.

content.label: Bottom line
content.text: Natural-image performance does not imply cross-domain robustness. For text and scientific imagery, visual plausibility can itself be a failure mode.

sections.title: Three domains, one reconstruction task
sections.body: EDSR, SwinIR, and a Stable Diffusion upscaler were evaluated at 2x reconstruction on DIV2K natural images, TextZoom document imagery, and STAR astronomical imagery. PSNR and SSIM captured fidelity; LPIPS added a view of diffusion outputs.

sections.title: Source-domain quality did not travel
sections.body: SwinIR led on DIV2K at 31.10 dB PSNR, but both conventional models fell to roughly 14.25 dB on TextZoom and 19.5 dB on STAR. The diffusion upscaler dropped to 5.65 dB on text, where plausible-looking output is not the same as correct output.

sections.title: Adaptation changed the conclusion
sections.body: Fine-tuned SwinIR reached 24.85 dB on TextZoom and 22.91 dB on STAR. The gap made the source of failure clearer: target domains were not necessarily too difficult, but their structure did not match the learned prior.

takeaway: In structured domains, visual plausibility can be a failure mode. Fidelity metrics, qualitative checks, and domain adaptation have to be evaluated together.

title: Fine-Tuning RoBERTa Under a One-Million-Parameter Budget
summary: Selective LoRA placement adapted RoBERTa to AG News with 796K trainable parameters.
intro: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning is not just a way to spend less compute. It is a design space in which adapter rank, target layers, and the evaluation path all matter.

content.title: Selective adaptation instead of full-model training
paragraphs: The task was AG News classification with a one-million-parameter trainable budget. Instead of updating the full RoBERTa base model, I froze it and placed LoRA adapters across early layers 0 and 1, a middle layer 5, and late layers 10 and 11.

That placement was deliberate: it left room to adjust lexical, intermediate, and task-specific representations while keeping the trainable footprint small. The final setup trained 796,420 parameters, around 0.63% of a fully trainable RoBERTa.

content.title: Training setup
items: LoRA rank 12 with alpha 32 and adapter dropout.
AdamW optimizer with cosine decay over five epochs.
Adapters placed in early, middle, and late layers instead of a broad uniform placement.
Evaluation tracked validation and inference paths separately.

content.title: Model variants
content.note: The targeted LoRA setup had the strongest validation result. The LoRA-plus-distillation variant had the best listed inference score, so the two results should not be collapsed into one winner.

content.title: The budget shaped the engineering
paragraphs: A parameter budget makes adapter placement part of the model design. Increasing the number of target layers is not automatically useful if it spends capacity where the task does not need it.

The result was not a claim that one narrow adapter layout is universally best. It was evidence that targeted adaptation can outperform a broader setup while training fewer than one percent of the base model.

content.label: What stayed useful
content.text: Under constraints, where adapters go can matter more than how many parameters are trainable.

sections.title: Target the adaptation
sections.body: Rather than updating the full base model, the experiment froze RoBERTa and placed LoRA adapters across early layers 0 and 1, middle layer 5, and late layers 10 and 11. That layout gave the model room to adjust lexical, intermediate, and task-specific representations.

sections.title: A small trainable footprint
sections.body: The final setup used rank 12, alpha 32, adapter dropout, AdamW, cosine decay, and five epochs. In total, it trained 796,420 parameters—about 0.63 percent of a fully trainable RoBERTa.

sections.title: Keep evaluation differences visible
sections.body: Targeted LoRA produced the best validation score at 92.97 percent accuracy, while a LoRA-plus-distillation variant posted the best listed inference score at 84.90 percent. Preserving that distinction is more useful than declaring one universal winner.

takeaway: Selective adaptation outperformed a broader setup with fewer trainable weights; under constraints, where adapters go can matter more than how many there are.

title: Designing a Compact ResNet for CIFAR-10
summary: A 4.17M-parameter ResNet made the tradeoff between validation performance and external generalization tangible.
intro: A compact classifier does not have to be simplistic. This experiment asked how far a careful ResNet-style design could go on 32 by 32 images while treating the parameter budget as a real constraint.

content.title: Design for 32 × 32 images
paragraphs: CIFAR-10 images are small enough that early max pooling throws away useful detail. The network begins with a 3 × 3 convolution with 32 filters and no initial max pool, then grows progressively through 32 → 64 → 128 → 192 → 256 channels.

The architecture uses four residual stages with two blocks each, global average pooling, batch normalization, and dropout. Inside a block, two 3 × 3 convolutions are followed by normalization, ReLU, and 0.2 dropout; a 1 × 1 shortcut handles dimension changes.

content.title: Where the parameter budget went
content.note: The final architecture has 4,167,850 parameters. Most capacity sits in the deeper stages, where the model learns higher-level visual features.

content.title: Training was part of the model
items: Random crops from padded 40 × 40 images, horizontal flips, and CIFAR-10 normalization.
Nesterov SGD with 0.9 momentum, 0.0005 weight decay, and a 120-epoch run.
Dropout, label smoothing at 0.1, gradient clipping at max norm 1.0, and mixed precision.
OneCycleLR: 0.01 to 0.1, then cosine annealing for final refinement.

content.title: Validation was not the whole story
paragraphs: Training accuracy reached 98.71% and validation accuracy reached 94.31%. The external Kaggle test score was 83.059%. The gap was an important result: one held-out split can make a model look more finished than it is.

The project stayed below the five-million-parameter target while making the accuracy-to-parameter tradeoff concrete. Progressive filter expansion, regularization, augmentation, and the schedule worked together; depth alone was not the explanation.

content.label: Caveat
content.text: The external test gap is a useful reminder that generalization needs to be checked outside the validation path, especially when a compact model looks highly tuned to one split.

sections.title: Design for the image size
sections.body: CIFAR-10 images are too small to discard detail with early max pooling. The network began with a 3 by 3 convolution and scaled channels gradually from 32 through 256, using two residual blocks per stage.

sections.title: Treat training as part of the model
sections.body: Dropout, batch normalization, random crops, horizontal flips, Nesterov SGD, label smoothing, mixed precision, gradient clipping, and a OneCycle schedule all contributed to the final behavior over 120 epochs.

sections.title: The useful caveat
sections.body: Validation accuracy reached 94.31 percent, while the Kaggle test score was 83.059 percent. That difference was an important result in itself: a single held-out split can make a model look more finished than it is.

takeaway: Generalization came from the entire training system, not depth alone—and it still needed an external test to be believed.

title: Building Singularity: An Agentic Research Platform That Stays Responsive
summary: The systems decisions behind a citation-grounded research platform that keeps long-running work visible and recoverable.
intro: An agentic research application is a systems problem as much as an AI problem. The central challenge was designing a dependable path from an open-ended question to a citation-grounded report while jobs run longer than a web request.

content.title: Research is planned, fanned out, and written bottom-up
paragraphs: Planner workers propose research plans from three perspectives. A plan manager compares them and produces the final plan. Research agents then receive targeted retrieval and analysis skills, fan out queries per section, and pass sources through credibility gating.

Writer and publisher agents work from leaf sections upward. Parent sections receive completed child content as context, so the report summarizes real work rather than outline stubs. The final pass refines the assembled report and keeps citations tied to the evidence path.

content.title: Agent skill layers
items: 18 retrieval skills spanning web, academic, PDF, code, dataset, legal, financial, and public data sources.
18 analysis skills including claim verification, contradiction detection, credibility scoring, synthesis, and quality checks.
8 output skills for report generation, bibliography, annotation, executive summaries, and visualization specifications.

content.title: Long-running work has to be observable
paragraphs: FastAPI writes a job to Redis through ARQ and returns immediately. The worker executes the research pipeline, publishes every phase transition through Redis Pub/Sub, and an SSE endpoint forwards progress to the browser. The API and worker are decoupled in lifecycle and can scale independently.

Worker startup runs orphan recovery: stale pending or running jobs are marked failed and publish an SSE error instead of spinning forever in the frontend. Idempotency keys return an existing job for duplicate submissions, while append-only report versions make retries and concurrent reads safer.

content.title: System boundaries
rows: Dashboard, report viewer, chat panel, BYOK profile
JWT/Google OAuth, rate limits, 31 REST + SSE endpoints
Jobs, reports, encrypted BYOK keys, usage records
Queue broker, progress events, sliding-window rate limiting
Per-run retrieval chunks and semantic search

content.label: The product boundary
content.text: Agents and retrieval make research useful. Queues, recovery, streaming, versioning, idempotency, and security boundaries are what make the work dependable when it runs longer than a request.

sections.title: Stage the research work
sections.body: Planner workers propose approaches from different perspectives before a plan manager combines them. Research agents then retrieve evidence, extract PDFs, assess credibility, detect contradictions, and synthesize section-level material.

sections.title: Write from leaves upward
sections.body: Leaf sections are written before their parents receive completed child content as context. Qdrant stores retrieved chunks as 384-dimensional embeddings so writers can retrieve evidence for the section in front of them instead of filling an outline with placeholders.

sections.title: Make long work observable
sections.body: The API writes a job to Redis and returns quickly; ARQ workers handle execution and publish progress through Redis Pub/Sub to Server-Sent Events. Startup recovery marks stale jobs as failed, while idempotency keys and an append-only report history make the workflow safer to retry.

takeaway: The agents and retrieval make the product useful; queues, recovery, streaming, versioning, and security boundaries are what make it feel dependable.

title: What a Small Math Model Taught Me About Answer Selection
summary: A generator–verifier–ranker system showed that majority vote still beat learned single-answer selection on GSM8K.
intro: The project began with a deceptively useful question: when a small model samples several math solutions, can a learned verifier choose the right one better than consensus? The answer revealed where the system was actually limited.

content.title: Separate generation from answer selection
paragraphs: SMOLSolver tests a small, modular system for GSM8K: a Phi-2 generator, an outcome-level RoBERTa-large verifier, a pairwise RoBERTa-large ranker, and consensus analysis. Each component can be trained, replaced, and evaluated independently.

The generator is Phi-2 (2.7B) fine-tuned with 4-bit NF4 QLoRA. It uses rank 16 adapters on q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, and o_proj, then samples 15 solutions per test question. Across 1,319 GSM8K questions, that produced 19,785 candidate solutions.

content.title: What each selector learned
items: The verifier receives a question and complete solution, then predicts whether the extracted final answer is correct.
The ranker uses masked mean pooling and MarginRankingLoss to score a correct solution above an incorrect solution for the same question.
Consensus groups split questions by the margin between the most and second-most frequent answers across 15 samples.

content.title: The negative result was the useful result
paragraphs: Majority vote was strongest overall. Ranker-weighted voting nearly matched it at 68.16%, but did not beat it. Direct top-score selection was much weaker: 41.17% for the classifier and 36.54% for the ranker.

The scores held useful evidence as weights, but not enough calibration to select one candidate reliably. The low-consensus group stayed difficult: the best method reached 32.37%. When the generator produced competing answer clusters, a more complex selector did not recover enough signal.

content.label: Where to improve
content.text: For this setup, generator stability is the bottleneck. Better answer extraction, multi-seed runs, calibration analysis, shared generated training data, and process-level supervision are more promising than another decision layer.

sections.title: Separate generation from selection
sections.body: A QLoRA-tuned Phi-2 generated 15 candidates for each GSM8K question. One RoBERTa-large model estimated outcome correctness, while another was trained with a pairwise margin-ranking objective to put correct solutions above incorrect ones.

sections.title: A negative result with a clear lesson
sections.body: Majority vote was strongest overall at 68.61 percent. Ranker-weighted voting approached it at 68.16 percent, but selecting the highest-scored individual candidate was far weaker: 41.17 percent for the classifier and 36.54 percent for the ranker.

sections.title: Consensus exposed the bottleneck
sections.body: Majority vote achieved 96.04 percent where samples agreed but only 32.13 percent where they did not. The learned scores contained useful evidence, yet they were not calibrated enough to rescue a generator that was producing competing answer clusters.

takeaway: Selector complexity cannot always compensate for instability upstream. Improving the generator's consistency looked more promising than adding another decision layer.

title: Building the MLOps Backbone for an Image-Captioning System
summary: An image-captioning project used to make the deployment, observability, artifact, and feedback paths as concrete as the model.
intro: Snap2Caption was a way to work through the machine-learning system around a model: reliable data pairs, training artifacts, deployment paths, monitoring, and feedback—not only a caption returned to a browser.

content.title: The project is an MLOps system, not a finished SaaS claim
paragraphs: Snap2Caption is built around an image-captioning workflow: preprocess InstaCities1M pairs, fine-tune LLaVA, track artifacts, provision infrastructure, deploy across environments, expose captioning and feedback APIs, and instrument the serving path.

The strongest work is the platform. The default branch does not fully serve the fine-tuned model, so I present the project as MLOps engineering rather than a finished production product. That boundary matters more than a stronger-sounding claim.

content.title: Data and training
items: Docker Compose ETL downloads data, matches image/caption files, normalizes city folders, creates splits, and uploads processed data through rclone.
Pair validation keeps only records where the image and caption exist together; mismatches corrupt image-text alignment rather than adding harmless noise.
Verified training uses the InstaCities1M New York subset with LLaVA-1.5-7B, 4-bit NF4 QLoRA, bfloat16 compute, and LoRA targets q_proj, k_proj, and v_proj.
A containerized branch adds OmegaConf, Hugging Face datasets, PEFT, MLflow logging, artifact storage, and conditional model registration.

content.title: Platform and delivery path
rows: MLflow, Postgres, MinIO, namespaces and PVCs
Helm charts for platform, staging, canary, production
ArgoCD and Argo Workflows with Kaniko image builds
content.note: MinIO is S3-compatible object storage on Chameleon/OpenStack. It is not an AWS S3 deployment.

content.title: Serving and feedback are separate claims
paragraphs: On main, the FastAPI route validates an uploaded image and returns a static caption placeholder. The stronger model_serving_endpoint branch accepts a base64 image, loads a LLaVA-Next base model, merges a LoRA adapter, runs GPU inference, and exposes Prometheus metrics.

The feedback API stores the user ID, image, generated caption, and feedback in MinIO under feedback/{uid}/. This is the first step of an active-learning loop: capture inputs, outputs, and human feedback for later review and retraining. It is not a complete retraining loop yet.

content.label: Operational takeaway
content.text: A model becomes a product when data pairs, artifacts, deployment, monitoring, feedback, and the limits of what is live are all treated as first-class parts of the system.

sections.title: Start with trustworthy multimodal data
sections.body: The Docker Compose pipeline downloads data, matches images to captions, normalizes folders, creates splits, and uploads processed material to object storage. Pairing checks mattered because a mismatched image-caption pair teaches the wrong relationship, not merely a noisier one.

sections.title: Move artifacts through environments
sections.body: Terraform provisioned Chameleon Cloud infrastructure; Ansible and Kubespray configured Kubernetes. Helm deployed MLflow, Postgres, MinIO, and persistent storage, while ArgoCD and Argo Workflows handled synchronization, image building, deployment, and promotion.

sections.title: Be precise about what is live
sections.body: The default branch returns a static caption placeholder rather than serving the fine-tuned LLaVA model. A separate serving branch adds GPU inference and metrics. Keeping that boundary visible makes the MLOps work more credible, not less.

takeaway: A model becomes a product only when its data, artifacts, feedback, and operational limits are treated as first-class parts of the system.
